documents: Rapetsoa et al. 2022, Near Surface Geophysics 20, 572-589 (published PDF)

entry.evidence: With the goal of testing cost-effective seismic methods for mineral exploration and mining

sequences.source_document: Rapetsoa et al. 2022, Near Surface Geophysics 20, 572-589 (published PDF)

steps.action: Frame the need to image faults, dykes and reefs ahead of mining, noting that surface 3D seismics and borehole seismics fail to resolve small structures in noisy mines.
steps.quote: These problems highlight the growing need for these geological structures to be identified ahead of mining.

steps.action: Take from other groups' work that in-mine seismics improves imaging resolution, while noting it is not established in deep South African mines.
steps.quote: in-mine seismics has proven useful in improving the imaging resolution of the mineral deposits and geological structures

steps.action: Measure ultrasonic P-wave velocities and Archimedes bulk densities of core samples of reefs and host rocks at atmospheric pressure.
steps.quote: Five P-wave velocity measurements were taken on each sample and an average was taken as the final velocity value

steps.action: Compute 1D synthetic seismograms from BH1 densities, velocities and depths with a 130 Hz Ricker wavelet, predicting reflections at the MR and UG2.
steps.quote: We used a Ricker wavelet with a dominant frequency of 130 Hz and a sampling rate of 0.25 ms to compute the seismograms

steps.action: Build a 2D geological model from boreholes and mine plans and run 2D acoustic finite-difference modelling to generate synthetic shot gathers with near-survey parameters.
steps.quote: The 2D acoustic finite-difference modelling was conducted to assist with the planning of the in-mine seismic surveys

steps.action: Design the survey after a preparatory site visit, using prior GPR and ERT results to place shots and receivers over the targets.
steps.quote: Information from the ground-penetrating radar and electrical resistivity tomography surveys conducted in the tunnel a few weeks prior assisted in designing our surveys

steps.action: Acquire seven 2D in-mine reflection profiles (about 0.6 km total), focusing on three collinear 115 m incline-tunnel segments P5 to P7.
steps.quote: In November 2020, seven 2D in-mine seismic profiles were acquired with a total length of about 0.6 km over known orebodies

steps.action: Test sources (24 kg weight drop vs 5 kg sledgehammer) and sensors (planted cabled geophones vs 4.5 Hz land streamer), then choose the sledgehammer and land streamer.
steps.quote: A day was spent testing different sources (24 kg accelerated weight drop (AWD) and a 5 kg sledgehammer)

steps.action: Test a range of sampling rates to check that guided waves and mine noise do not contaminate the records; choose 0.25 ms.
steps.quote: A range of sampling rate parameters were also tested to ensure that guided waves and other mine-related noise

steps.action: Apply a processing workflow (geometry merge, statics, bandpass, top mute, f-k filter, NMO, residual statics, DMO, stack, Kirchhoff migration) to suppress mine noise.
steps.quote: The main aim of the processing workflow was to preserve primary reflections and remove source-generated and ambient noise

steps.action: Compare synthetic, raw and processed shot gathers: R1 (MR) and R2 (UG2) match the synthetics, and an unmodelled reflection R3 appears at 55 ms.
steps.quote: Some reflections (R1 and R2) observed in the raw shot gathers (red arrows in Fig. 5b, e) matched reflections in the synthetic shot gathers

steps.action: Invert first-break picks for a refraction velocity model, then after tests on velocity fields migrate and depth-convert the stack at 5500 m/s.
steps.quote: The picks were inverted for the two-layer-based refraction model, with four iterations and an RMS error of 1.45–2.00 ms.

steps.action: Interpret R3 as the UG1 chromitite, while naming wavefield effects of side tunnels, fractures and infrastructure as unexcluded alternatives.
steps.quote: R3 is interpreted to originate from the UG1, which is a chromitite mineralization that is well known in other mines within the Bushveld Complex.

steps.action: Check the tomographic velocities against published velocities and borehole stratigraphy.
steps.quote: These velocities show a good match with the known velocities from (norite and pyroxenite; Manzi et al., 2020)

steps.action: Overlay the BH1 log and 1D synthetic on the migrated depth section, tying R1 to the MR at about 55 m and R2 to the UG2 at about 124 m.
steps.quote: Overlaying the borehole log and 1D synthetic data onto the depth-converted migrated section (Fig. 8b) confirms that the strong reflections (R1)

steps.action: Interpret folding, faults f1 to f7, dykes and an IRUP disrupting the reflectors, and infer that the faults were active after reef deposition.
steps.quote: MR and UG2 are affected by folding (e.g., a synclinal structure is observed between CDP 160 and 200)

steps.action: Compute vertical (about 10.5 m) and post-migration horizontal (about 21 m) resolution limits, and argue that thin reefs are imaged through impedance proxies.
steps.quote: This gives us the vertical resolution limit of ∼ 10.5 m

steps.action: Check reflector depths against borehole intersections (BH1, BH2) and the mine orebody models in a 3D integration.
steps.quote: Generally, the seismic data has a good tie (within 3 m discrepancy) with the borehole information (Fig. 10a).

steps.action: Attribute the 0 to 3 m depth mismatches to auxiliaries (borehole projection, depth-conversion velocity, poorly constrained orebody models) rather than to the reflector identification.
steps.quote: The minor discrepancies (0–3 m) in depth positions between seismics, orebodies and borehole data might be due to three reasons

steps.action: Keep the structural interpretation: known faults and dykes (RFZ, dyke 2) confirmed, plus new faults and dykes absent from the mine model.
steps.quote: our results confirm the existence of previously known faults and dykes

steps.action: Propose revising the mine orebody model, since seismics suggest that MR and UG2 continue, faulted, west of the outcrop position.
steps.quote: This suggests that MR and UG2 are continuous on the western side of the outcrop position, which contradicts the geometry shown in the mine orebodies

steps.action: Conclude that low-cost in-mine seismics (sledgehammer plus land streamer) images the reefs and structures and costs over 60% less than commercial surface surveys.
steps.quote: the results demonstrate that in-mine seismic surveys can be an asset for mineral exploration and mining

tree.answer: Reflections from MR and UG2 reefs and crosscutting structures beneath the tunnel
No; thin reefs are imaged by seismics, the MR only through hangingwall/footwall impedance proxies
Test whether cost-effective in-mine seismics can image the reefs and structures
Only for R3: UG1 versus wavefield artifacts; no formal rivals for R1/R2
Synthetic gathers predict R1/R2 travel times from borehole-based models
Found: survey run in existing tunnels of a mine under care and maintenance
Borehole ties within 3 m at two boreholes; velocities match published values
MR and UG2 imaged with confidence; R3 as UG1 left inconclusive

end.claim: Low-cost in-mine 2D reflection seismics imaged the Merensky Reef and UG2 about 55 m and 124 m below the tunnel floor, tied to boreholes within 3 m, and delineated crosscutting faults and dykes.

decisive_move.sentence: Tying the migrated depth section to the BH1 log and synthetic seismogram (and then BH2) is what identifies R1 as the MR and R2 as the UG2; without it the reflections would be unassigned.

gates.evidence: Survey placement was guided by known targets and by synthetic modelling run to plan the survey (p. 577), but no hypothesis directed acquisition. The reef identification faced a borehole tie it could have failed (pp. 583, 585), while R3 and the new faults were not tested. The synthetic predictions predate the data, but processing parameters (velocity fields, filters) were chosen after viewing the data (p. 582).

imports.item: Archimedes' principle (water-immersion method) for bulk density
UK1401 SURFER ultrasonic tester for P-wave velocity

novelty_claims.quote: The application of in-mine seismic techniques has grown worldwide; however, the techniques are not yet well established in deep South African mines.
this work has identified more faults (e.g., f1–f7 in Figs 9 and 10c, d) and dykes
R3 is not modelled in the synthetic data (Figs 4 and 5a) as it was not known
The study forms a pilot concept for the mining industry to utilize in-mine seismics development and mine planning.

limits: Headline status capability_characterized. Sub-claims: R3 as UG1 is at most best_explanation, and the authors call it not conclusive (p. 583). The new faults f1-f7, the dykes and the IRUP are best_explanation interpretations without drilling confirmation, and fault throws are below resolution (p. 587). Western continuity of MR/UG2 is conditional, 'if our interpretation is correct' (p. 587). The >60% cost saving is asserted without a cost breakdown (p. 587). Only P5-P7 of seven profiles are reported, and the surface active/passive data are excluded (pp. 580, 587). The comparison set is partly circular: the synthetic model and the mine orebody model are built from the same boreholes used for the tie (inference). Processing parameters were chosen by inspection of the data, and alternative velocity fields are not reported (p. 582). Composition coded capability_first with reservation: the question (imaging known reefs) preceded the capability test, so the walk is a capability demonstration on known targets rather than capability followed by question (inference). No review file supplied; the acknowledgements mention two reviewers, but their requests are unknown.

disagreements.target: Commercial surface seismic surveys with vibroseis and many receivers
disagreements.support: Cost comparison asserted for the sledgehammer and land-streamer set-up, without itemised figures.
disagreements.quote: approximately > 60% cheaper than if the survey was acquired by commercial contractors on surface

alternatives_considered.reason: AWD unsafe given loose hanging wall and sidewall; sledgehammer light and low cost

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Planted cabled geophones (100 Hz horizontal, 14 Hz vertical)
alternatives_considered.reason: Planting took half a day per profile; land streamer quick and better coupled
Better results given resonant and spurious sensor frequencies

alternatives_considered.chosen: Constant 5500 m/s for migration and time-to-depth conversion
alternatives_considered.reason: Provided the best migrated sections; consistent with published velocities

alternatives_considered.chosen: Velocity measurements at atmospheric pressure, no porosity measurements
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Measurements at elevated pressures (20-60 MPa); porosity measurements
alternatives_considered.reason: Porosity comparable in crystalline rocks; none given for the pressure choice

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Wavefield effects from side tunnels, fracture systems, rock mass and mine infrastructure
alternatives_considered.reason: UG1 well known in other Bushveld mines
